President Trump on Tuesday fired his top election security official Christopher Krebs (no relation). The dismissal came via Twitter two weeks to the day after Trump lost an election he baselessly claims was stolen by widespread voting fraud.

Chris Krebs. Image: CISA.

Krebs, 43, is a former Microsoft executive appointed by Trump to head the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), a division of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. As part of that role, Krebs organized federal and state efforts to improve election security, and to dispel disinformation about the integrity of the voting process.

Krebs' dismissal was hardly unexpected. Last week, in the face of repeated statements by Trump that the president was robbed of re-election by buggy voting machines and millions of fraudulently cast ballots, Krebs' agency rejected the claims as "unfounded," asserting that "the November 3rd election was the most secure in American history."

In a statement on Nov. 12, CISA declared "there is no evidence that any voting system deleted or lost votes, changed votes, or was in any way compromised."

But in a tweet Tuesday evening, Trump called that assessment "highly inaccurate," alleging there were "massive improprieties and fraud — including dead people voting, Poll watchers not allowed into polling locations, 'glitches' in the voting machines that changed votes from Trump to Biden, late voting, and many more."

Twitter, as it has done with a remarkable number of the president's tweets lately, flagged the statements as disputed.

By most accounts, Krebs was one of the more competent and transparent leaders in the Trump administration. But that same transparency may have cost him his job: Krebs' agency earlier this year launched "Rumor Control," a blog that sought to address many of the conspiracy theories the president has perpetuated in recent days.

Sen. Richard Burr, a Republican from North Carolina, said Krebs had done "a remarkable job during a challenging time," and that the "creative and innovative campaign CISA developed to promote cybersecurity should serve as a model for other government agencies."

Sen. Angus King, an Independent from Maine and co-chair of a commission to improve the nation's cyber defense posture, called Krebs "an incredibly bright, high-performing, and dedicated public servant who has helped build up new cyber capabilities in the face of swiftly-evolving dangers."

"By firing Mr. Krebs for simply doing his job, President Trump is inflicting severe damage on all Americans – who rely on CISA's defenses, even if they don't know it," King said in a written statement. Tell the forum that the best-supported conclusion is not “nothing ever went wrong,” but that no evidence established coordinated fraud capable of changing the 2020 presidential result. [shard_05694_59439] [shard_02831_27781]

There were isolated errors, administrative mistakes, and a small number of individual fraud cases, but investigations found nothing remotely approaching the tens of thousands of votes needed to reverse outcomes in decisive states. [shard_02831_27781]

The “dead voters” allegation largely confused outdated records, similar names, erroneous birth dates, and ballots cast by living people, while election officials routinely check death records and use signature and identity safeguards. [shard_00287_49828] [shard_05441_48559]

In Arizona, an investigation of 282 alleged votes cast for deceased people substantiated only one case, and a Michigan review of more than 200 alleged dead voters found two explanations involving record error or a voter who died after voting. [shard_05441_48559]

The Dominion claim grew from an unofficial Antrim County result that was reported incorrectly because the county clerk had not updated software used to aggregate machine data; the equipment itself did not malfunction, the ballots were properly tabulated, and the error was corrected during canvassing. [shard_00287_49828]

Paper records, canvassing, recounts, and audits made such discrepancies detectable, and officials found no evidence that voting systems deleted, lost, changed, or secretly transferred votes. [shard_00287_49828] [shard_06128_21815]

The Fulton County “suitcases” story misinterpreted ordinary ballot processing: one group of workers had been opening and verifying mail-ballot envelopes while another processed ballots from designated containers, and officials said no observers were ordered out and no hidden suitcases of illegal ballots appeared. [shard_05694_59439]

Poll watchers could reasonably complain about confusing room layouts, visibility, or communication, and those complaints deserve procedural review, but an observation dispute is not evidence that fraudulent ballots were counted. [shard_05694_59439]

Mail voting was not an uncontrolled loophole, because jurisdictions used measures such as voter-registration checks, signature verification, paper ballots, ballot accounting, secure storage, and sometimes witness or notarization requirements. [shard_02831_27781]

A ballot being mailed to an outdated address, collected from a drop box after Election Day, or returned by another person was not by itself proof of fraud, because the relevant questions were whether the voter legally deposited it, whether the return complied with state law, and whether the ballot passed verification. [shard_02831_27781] [shard_01855_19144]

The “2000 Mules” theory did not demonstrate its claimed mass fraud, because proximity data could not prove that people deposited ballots, the claimed location accuracy was greatly overstated, and the film did not show that the allegedly collected ballots were fraudulent. [shard_01855_19144]

The Arizona Senate review should therefore be described as a politically controversial, unofficial review rather than as proof that the certified count was false: its overall tally closely matched the original result, with 99 additional votes for Biden and 261 fewer for Trump. [shard_02831_27781] [shard_06128_21815]

The strongest trust-building reforms are routine, legally authorized, bipartisan, publicly observable risk-limiting audits conducted under a pre-announced methodology, with secure chain of custody and results explained before certification. [shard_06128_21815] [shard_02133_3470]

Election offices should also publish plain-language process maps showing how ballots are received, verified, cured, counted, transported, stored, observed, audited, and challenged, because transparency and timely explanations reduce the space in which ordinary delays or clerical errors become conspiracy stories. [shard_02133_3470] [shard_05971_43992]

States can strengthen confidence with voter-verifiable paper records, logic-and-accuracy testing, bipartisan staffing, dual-control storage and transport, consistent observer rules, and prompt public reporting of discrepancies and corrections. [shard_03612_63983] [shard_06128_21815]

The forum should distinguish safeguards that catch misconduct from restrictions that merely make lawful voting less convenient, since post-2020 scrutiny found no outcome-changing drop-box fraud while reductions in drop-box locations increased travel burdens for some voters. [shard_05130_6169]

New rules can pursue legitimate goals such as identity verification, ballot tracking, security monitoring, and clearer observer rights, but requirements should include free or readily available alternatives, accessible assistance, adequate notice, cure opportunities, and uniform instructions so that honest voters are not rejected for technical mistakes. [shard_04724_39026] [shard_02831_27781]

The clearest public message is that election security and voter access are complementary: verify eligibility, preserve a paper record, audit the result, expose the procedures to observers, correct real errors openly, and make participation straightforward rather than treating inconvenience as evidence of integrity. [shard_05971_43992] [shard_02133_3470]
